638.title: The Khalsa's greeting
638.hook: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh: the Khalsa belongs to God, and so does the victory
638.howItsDone: Many Sikhs greet one another, and open talks in the gurdwara, with Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh; the listener replies with the same words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jaikara, and your line: sat sri akaal. Who did you greet with it? Today, a second Sikh greeting, longer and with a twist at the end. Day six hundred thirty-eight.

A speaker steps up to the microphone in a gurdwara. Before a single word of the talk, they put their palms together and say: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. And the whole congregation says it straight back to them, word for word. Only then does the talk begin. Two friends meet at the door afterward and say the same thing, sometimes shortened to just fateh. It sounds like a formality. It's actually a small statement about who wins.
screen: `A SPEAKER AT THE MICROPHONE.` → `THE HALL SAYS IT BACK.` → `A STATEMENT ABOUT WHO WINS.`

segments.voice: Take the two halves. Waheguru ji ka Khalsa: the Khalsa belongs to Waheguru. The Khalsa is the community of initiated Sikhs that Guru Gobind Singh founded at Anandpur on Vaisakhi in 1699, and the word khalsa carries the sense of pure, belonging directly to the sovereign with no middleman. Then Waheguru ji ki fateh: the victory belongs to Waheguru. Fateh means victory, a word Punjabi took from Persian and Arabic. Sikh tradition links this greeting to the founding of the Khalsa, and it's the greeting many Sikhs, especially initiated Sikhs, use with one another. Now, the twist. A greeting about victory could easily turn into bragging: we win. This one does the opposite. It hands the victory away the moment it's spoken. Whatever goes well today, the exam, the deal, the hard conversation, the battle in older times, it isn't mine. It's Waheguru's. And the people saying it don't belong to themselves either. They belong to Waheguru too. So two people greeting each other this way are reminding each other, every single time, of two things: you are not your own, and the credit is not yours. That could sound heavy. In practice it's freeing. If the victory is God's, then so, in a way, is the pressure. A person can work as hard as they're able and then let the outcome rest where it belongs. And notice it's said back, word for word. Neither person is above the other in this greeting. Both are equally God's.
screen: `THE KHALSA: FOUNDED 1699.` · `KHALSA: BELONGING TO GOD.` · `FATEH: VICTORY.` · `HANDING THE VICTORY AWAY.` · then, large: `THE VICTORY IS HIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of one thing that went well for you recently, something you might be quietly proud of. Picture it clearly. Now, without dismissing your effort, imagine handing the credit forward: to the people who helped, to the chances you were given, and, if you pray, to the One. Notice whether that feels like a loss or a relief. Then, if you're comfortable, say the greeting once, softly: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. Later today, greet someone with fateh, or with your own warm hello. The bell holds the time.
Fateh. Victory. In the Khalsa's greeting, Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh, both the community and the victory belong to God.
Your line: the victory is his. Today, when something goes right, say thank you to someone else before you take the credit. Day six hundred thirty-eight.

639.title: Ardas before a meal
639.hook: families say a short Ardas before eating, and in the gurdwara food is offered with an Ardas before it's served
639.howItsDone: In the gurdwara, langar and karah prashad are offered with an Ardas before being served; at home, many Sikh families say a short Ardas or simply Waheguru before eating.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fateh, and your line: the victory is his. Did you pass the credit on to someone? This week the Ardas leaves the gurdwara hall and comes home, starting at the table. Day six hundred thirty-nine.

The plates are down. The dal is steaming, the rotis are stacked under a cloth, and someone's younger brother already has one hand moving. In many Sikh homes, that hand gets a gentle look. Wait. Someone stands, or just folds their hands at the table, and says a short Ardas, sometimes only a few lines, sometimes just Waheguru and a thank-you. Then everyone eats. It takes less than a minute. It happens in kitchens all over the world, every day.
screen: `THE DAL IS STEAMING.` → `ONE HAND ALREADY MOVING.` → `WAIT: A SHORT ARDAS.`

segments.voice: The Ardas we've been walking through line by line is long. But the Ardas isn't only for the gurdwara, and it isn't only the full form. Sikhs pray it short when the moment is short. Before food, the idea is simple: thank the Giver before taking the gift. In the gurdwara, this is done with care. Before langar is served, food from the kitchen is often brought before the Guru Granth Sahib and an Ardas is said over it. Karah prashad, the sweet offering everyone receives, is also blessed with an Ardas, and in many gurdwaras a kirpan is touched to it before it's shared. Only then does the food go out. Even the full Ardas remembers the kitchen. Among the things it asks for is deg teg fateh. Deg is the cooking pot, the cauldron of the free kitchen. Teg is the sword. Victory to both: to the pot that feeds anyone who comes, and to the sword that protects the weak. Food is so central to Sikh life that it sits in the same breath as defense. At home it's simpler. Families vary: a few lines of the Ardas, a quiet Waheguru, a moment of folded hands. What stays the same is the pause. The food is treated as given, not just bought. That pause does something to the meal itself. A plate you've thanked for is hard to waste. It's a little harder to eat in a rush, or in front of a screen. And it reminds the people at the table that somewhere, a langar is serving strangers the same dal.
screen: `THANK THE GIVER BEFORE THE GIFT.` · `LANGAR IS OFFERED FIRST.` · `DEG TEG FATEH: POT AND SWORD.` · `AT HOME: THE PAUSE.` · then, large: `THANKS BEFORE FOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, a rehearsal for your next meal. Picture the next plate you'll eat from. Picture where it came from: the field, the truck, the store, the hands that cooked it, even if those hands were yours. Let one face come to mind among all those people. Then let yourself feel grateful, plainly, without needing the right words. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, or a line you already know. When the food actually arrives today, pause for one breath before the first bite. The bell holds the time.
Ardas before a meal. Sikhs offer food with an Ardas before it's served in the gurdwara, and many families pause at home with a short Ardas or Waheguru before eating.
Your line: thanks before food. Today, before every meal, even a snack at your desk, pause for one breath and name who it came from. Day six hundred thirty-nine.

640.title: Ardas before a journey
640.hook: before travel, exams or new work, Sikhs ask for help in Ardas
640.howItsDone: Before travel, exams, a new job or another undertaking, many Sikhs say a short Ardas at home or ask for one at the gurdwara, sometimes offering karah prashad, asking that the task be brought to a good end.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ardas before a meal, and your line: thanks before food. Did you pause before a bite? Today the Ardas walks out the front door with you. Day six hundred forty.

The suitcase is zipped. The car is running in the driveway, or the ride is two minutes away. A student has an exam at nine. Someone is starting a new job on Monday and hasn't slept well all weekend. In many Sikh families, before anyone walks out, there's a moment. Hands fold. A short Ardas is said, sometimes by a grandparent, sometimes by the traveler. Sometimes the family goes to the gurdwara first and asks for the Ardas there. Then, and only then, the door opens.
screen: `THE SUITCASE IS ZIPPED.` → `AN EXAM AT NINE.` → `HANDS FOLD BEFORE THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Every full Ardas already asks for this. Near the end comes the line sarbat de kaaraj raas karne: make everyone's tasks succeed. Kaaraj is a task, a piece of work, an undertaking. Raas means set right, brought to a good end. It's a general request, for everybody. Before a journey, an exam, a wedding, a surgery or a new business, Sikhs make it specific: this trip, this test, this first day. Families sometimes offer karah prashad at the gurdwara so the Ardas can be said there, with the congregation joining in. There's a line in the Guru Granth Sahib that many Sikhs know by heart for exactly these moments. In Sri Rag ki Var, on ang 91, it says, in effect: whatever work you want done, speak of it to the Lord; the True Guru will set it right, and you have His word on it. Notice what this asking is and isn't. It isn't a lucky charm, and it isn't a way to skip the studying. Sikh teaching expects honest effort: you still pack, still prepare, still drive carefully. The Ardas puts the effort and the outcome in the right order. You do the work. You place the result in the hands of the One. And then you go, lighter. There's a practical gift in that, too. Saying a task out loud, before you start, makes you name what you're actually walking into. Half of nerves is not knowing what you're afraid of. A short Ardas makes it plain: this is the road, this is what I hope for, this is in Your hands.
screen: `SARBAT DE KAARAJ RAAS KARNE.` · `NAME THIS TRIP, THIS TEST.` · `SPEAK OF IT TO THE LORD.` · `EFFORT FIRST, OUTCOME GIVEN.` · then, large: `ASK BEFORE YOU GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of your very next real task: a call, a drive, a meeting, a page of homework. Picture yourself just before starting it. Now name it, plainly, in one sentence: this is what I'm about to do. Add one more: this is what I hope for. Notice what loosens in you once it's said. If you pray, you can place it before the One in your own words, or simply say Waheguru. If not, let the naming itself be the pause. Then, when the sit ends, begin that task. The bell holds the time.
Ardas before a journey. Before travel, exams, new work, Sikhs name the task in Ardas and ask that it be brought to a good end: kaaraj raas.
Your line: ask before you go. Today, before you leave the house or start something hard, stop at the door for one breath and name what you're walking into. Day six hundred forty.

641.title: Ardas in grief
641.hook: the Ardas for the dead asks peace for the one who has gone, and for those left, the strength to accept the Will
641.howItsDone: After a death, Sikhs sing Kirtan Sohila at the cremation, often hold a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and close it with an Ardas asking rest for the departed and acceptance of the Will for the family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ardas before a journey, and your line: ask before you go. What did you name before you started? Today, the hardest door the Ardas walks through. Go gently. Day six hundred forty-one.

A family stands in a gurdwara a few days after a funeral. Some of them haven't slept. Someone is holding a framed photo; someone else is holding a toddler who doesn't understand why everyone is so quiet. In the days since the death, the Guru Granth Sahib has been read, perhaps from beginning to end. Now the reading is finished. The congregation rises, and the Ardas begins. And somewhere in it, the name of the one who died is spoken aloud, for the last time in this way.
screen: `A FAMILY, A FEW DAYS AFTER.` → `THE READING IS FINISHED.` → `THE NAME IS SPOKEN ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Sikhs usually cremate their dead. At the cremation, and again each night at home, Kirtan Sohila, the evening hymns, is sung. Over the following days, many families hold a reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, and when it ends, an Ardas is said that many call the antim ardas, the final prayer. The petition in that Ardas asks two things. First, for the one who has gone: that their soul find rest, a place at the Guru's feet, union with the One. Second, for the ones left: the strength to accept the Will. That word, will, is bhaana. It runs all through Sikh teaching. Bhaana mannan, accepting the Will, is one of the hardest and most honored things a Sikh can do. Guru Arjan put it in a line many grieving families hold onto. In Raag Asa, on ang 394, he says, in effect: what You do seems sweet to me; Nanak asks only for the treasure of the Name. Now, an honest note. Accepting the Will doesn't mean pretending it doesn't hurt. Sikh teaching discourages loud wailing and ritual mourning displays, and it treats death as part of the One's order rather than a punishment. But it doesn't forbid tears. Accepting the Will is something people grow into, sometimes over years, and the Ardas doesn't demand that it be finished by Sunday. It asks for the strength to keep moving toward it. And notice: the family isn't asked to do this alone. The whole congregation stands with them, and the line rising spirits, good for all, is said even here.
screen: `KIRTAN SOHILA AT THE CREMATION.` · `REST FOR THE ONE WHO HAS GONE.` · `BHAANA: THE WILL.` · `ACCEPTANCE TAKES TIME.` · then, large: `IN HIS WILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and take it at whatever depth feels right today. Bring to mind someone you miss: a grandparent, a friend, even a pet, or someone who isn't gone but is far away. Let their face come. If it hurts, let it hurt a little. Breathe. Then, if you pray, you can ask peace for them, and the strength to accept what you can't change, in your own words or with a quiet Waheguru. If not, simply wish them peace. Stay with them until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Ardas in grief. After a death, the Ardas asks rest for the one who has gone, and for the family, the strength to accept the Will, bhaana.
Your line: in his will. Today, if you know someone who is grieving, send them one line, just that you're thinking of them. Nothing to fix. Day six hundred forty-one.

642.title: Ardas in joy
642.hook: births, weddings and new homes all get an Ardas of thanks
642.howItsDone: Sikhs mark births, weddings, new homes and other blessings with a shukrana, an Ardas of thanks, often with a reading, karah prashad and the singing of Anand Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ardas in grief, and your line: in his will. Did you send someone a line? Today, the same prayer at the opposite end of life's weather. Day six hundred forty-two.

Here's a question worth asking yourself honestly: when do you pray, or reach for something bigger, more often, when things are falling apart or when they're going well? For many people it's the first. Trouble sends us looking. Good news sends us to the group chat. Sikh life has a deliberate counterweight to that. A baby is born: there's an Ardas. A wedding: there's an Ardas at the start and at the end. A new home, a new shop, a new job that finally came through: an Ardas. Not asking for anything. Just saying thank you.
screen: `WHEN DO YOU REACH UPWARD?` → `TROUBLE SENDS US LOOKING.` → `GOOD NEWS GETS AN ARDAS TOO.`

segments.voice: Punjabi has a word for this: shukrana, thanksgiving, from the Persian word for thanks. A shukrane di ardas is a prayer of thanks, and it uses the same frame as every Ardas, with the petition simply turned into gratitude. Look at how joy gets marked. When a baby is born, the family often brings the child to the gurdwara. An Ardas of thanks is said, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random, and the first letter of the hymn on that page, the hukamnama, guides the choice of the child's name. At a wedding, the Anand Karaj, the ceremony begins with an Ardas, the couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib four times, and it ends with an Ardas again. When a family moves into a new home, many hold a reading, often of Sukhmani Sahib, and close it with an Ardas, sometimes with karah prashad for everyone who came. In nearly every one of these, you'll also hear Anand Sahib, the song of bliss by Guru Amar Das, on ang 917. It opens, in effect: joy has come, my mother, for I have found the True Guru. The Rehat Maryada has it sung at weddings and other ceremonies, and a short portion closes most congregational gatherings. Why make such a point of thanks? Because in Sikh teaching, the good things are gifts from the One just as surely as the hard things are within the Will. If grief is met with acceptance, joy is met with gratitude. Both keep a person's eyes on the Giver, not only on the gift.
screen: `SHUKRANA: THANKSGIVING.` · `A BIRTH: A NAME FROM THE HUKAM.` · `A WEDDING BEGINS AND ENDS IN ARDAS.` · `ANAND SAHIB: JOY HAS COME.` · then, large: `THANKS IN JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Find one joy from the last week. It doesn't have to be big: a good meal, a text from an old friend, a morning when your knee didn't ache. Bring it back as clearly as you can. Where were you? Who was there? Let yourself feel it again. Now, instead of moving on, stay. If you pray, you can say thank you to the One for it, in your own words, or with a single Waheguru. If not, simply hold the gratitude, without asking for anything more. The bell holds the time.
Ardas in joy. Births, weddings, new homes and answered hopes all get a shukrana, an Ardas of thanks, often with Anand Sahib, the song of bliss.
Your line: thanks in joy. Today, when something good happens, before you post it or text it, pause and say thanks first. Day six hundred forty-two.

643.title: Why standing
643.hook: the Ardas is said standing: readiness and respect, like standing before a king
643.howItsDone: Sikhs stand for the Ardas with hands joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, often after reciting 'tu thakur tum peh ardaas' from Sukhmani Sahib; those who cannot stand join seated.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ardas in joy, and your line: thanks in joy. What good thing did you thank for first? Today, not the words of the Ardas but the body that says them. Day six hundred forty-three.

A judge walks into a courtroom and everyone rises. A national anthem starts and a stadium full of people stands up, even the ones holding nachos. A teacher walks into some classrooms, in some countries, and thirty kids get to their feet. Standing is one of the oldest ways humans have of saying: this matters, and I'm paying attention. In the gurdwara, when it's time for the Ardas, the whole congregation stands. Hands are folded. Faces turn toward the Guru Granth Sahib. Nobody needs to be told why.
screen: `ALL RISE.` → `A STADIUM ON ITS FEET.` → `THE CONGREGATION STANDS.`

segments.voice: That's why the Ardas is so often called the standing prayer. Sikhs give a few reasons for the posture, and they fit together. The first is respect. Sikhs speak of the Guru as the true king, sacha paatshah. In the courts of Punjab's rulers, you didn't present a petition sitting down. You stood, hands joined, and made your request. The Ardas, a petition, is made the same way before the Guru Granth Sahib. The second is readiness. Someone sitting is resting. Someone standing can move. Sikh history is full of people who stood up for others, and the posture keeps that in the body: whatever is asked for in the Ardas, the one asking is ready to act on it. The third is togetherness. When everyone stands, nobody is above anyone else. The donor and the person who came for langar are on their feet side by side. Just before the Ardas begins, many congregations recite a line from Sukhmani Sahib, on ang 268. It says, in effect: You are the Master, to You is this prayer; body and soul are all Your gift. It's spoken standing, and it sets the tone: not a list of demands, but servants presenting themselves. One more thing, plainly. The posture is a custom of respect, not a test. People who can't stand, the elderly, the sick, someone with a baby asleep on their lap, join the Ardas sitting, and they're no less part of it. Standing is what the heart is doing. The legs just help when they can.
screen: `RESPECT: BEFORE THE TRUE KING.` · `READINESS: READY TO ACT.` · `TOGETHERNESS: NOBODY ABOVE.` · `ANG 268: YOU ARE THE MASTER.` · then, large: `STAND READY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand once. If you're able, get up now. Feet a little apart, weight even. If you want, fold your hands in front of your chest. Notice how standing feels different from sitting: more awake, a little more exposed, more ready. Breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, standing, and let that be your whole prayer for now. If you can't stand, sit up tall and let your spine do the standing. Stay there until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Why standing. The Ardas is said standing, hands joined: respect before the true king, readiness to act, and everyone equal on their feet.
Your line: stand ready. Today, when someone asks for help, stand up to answer: from your chair, from the couch. Let your body say yes first. Day six hundred forty-three.

644.title: Your own petition
644.hook: putting a short personal request into your own words, the way Sikhs do inside the Ardas
644.howItsDone: Sikhs place their own request into the Ardas at the petition, in Punjabi or any language; at home a person praying alone names their reason in their own words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why standing, and your line: stand ready. Did you get up to answer someone? Today, the week ends with the most personal part of the Ardas. Day six hundred forty-four.

Most of the Ardas is inherited. The words about the ten Gurus, the martyrs, the gurdwaras left behind, rising spirits and good for all: these come down through generations, the same in a village in Punjab and a suburb in California. But there's one part no one can write for you. The petition. The reason today. It can be said in Punjabi, in English, in a whisper, in the words of a seven-year-old asking for her cat to get better. And it's still Ardas.
screen: `MOST OF THE ARDAS IS INHERITED.` → `ONE PART NO ONE CAN WRITE FOR YOU.` → `IN ANY LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Sikh teaching has never treated personal asking as something embarrassing. Guru Nanak says it plainly in the Japji, in the fourth pauri, on ang 2: we speak, we beg, give, give, and the Giver gives. The asking is expected. What Sikhs often add is a sense of how to ask. A petition is called a benti, a humble request. Not a demand, not a bargain, not a list of grievances. Think back over this week. Fateh: the victory belongs to God, so you don't have to pretend you control the outcome. The Ardas before a meal: begin with thanks. Before a journey: name the task honestly. In grief: ask for the strength to accept the Will, not only for the pain to stop. In joy: thanks, with nothing added. Standing: come ready to act on what you ask. Put those together and you have something like a shape for a personal petition, without anyone handing you the words. First, what you're thankful for. Then, what you're actually asking, plainly. Then, who else it's for, because the Ardas always widens. Some Sikhs also add a line of acceptance, that whatever comes is within the Will. The words themselves are yours. Nobody grades them. Ardas said in clumsy English by a teenager at 2 a.m. is still Ardas. And Sikhs often say the honest, clumsy version is closer to the point than a beautiful one that isn't meant.
screen: `WE BEG, AND THE GIVER GIVES.` · `BENTI: A HUMBLE REQUEST.` · `THANKS, ASK, WIDEN, ACCEPT.` · `CLUMSY AND HONEST IS ENOUGH.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: three lines. If you have paper or your phone's notes, use them. If not, compose in your head. Line one: something you're thankful for, today, specifically. Line two: the one thing you most want to ask for, said plainly. Line three: someone else this is for, or someone else who needs the same. Don't polish. Don't make it sound holy. Just make it true. If you pray, you can offer those lines inside your own prayer, or after a quiet Waheguru. If not, simply read them back to yourself. The bell holds the time.
Your own petition. Inside the inherited Ardas, the reason for today is said in your own words: a benti, a humble request, in any language.
Your line: your own words. Today, keep your three lines with you, and read them once more before you sleep. Day six hundred forty-four.

original.note: Gurmukhi: a humble request or supplication; in Gurbani often spelled ਬੇਨੰਤੀ.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Ardas is a fixed prayer you recite.
what it means: the inherited Ardas holds a place for your own words, in any language.
what a scholar hears: the fixed liturgy and the free petition sit side by side; Gurbani's word benti frames asking as humble request, and the Japji takes asking for granted.
